title: Overnight rundown - Dexter Lin candidate handoff
body:
Context:
- Interview loop for backend/runtime role (focused on latency optimizations, KV cache management). Candidate: Dexter Lin (senior infra/runtime engineer). 60-minute loop + 30 minutes pairing. I took notes during the pairing and then did a quick synthesis for on-call/takeaway team.

Quick take (one-sentence):
- Leaning toward move-forward for a second technical deep dive, but flagging 2 concerns (concurrency design assumptions and sparse testing). Candidate has strong intuition, pragmatic tradeoffs, but needs a clearer ownership story for long-term reliability.

High-level summary (bulleted):
- Background: 7 years infra, ex-search and ex-streaming company. Recent work: built a custom RPC multiplexor and a KV-backed caching layer for a recommendation service.
- Strengths: systemic debugging, careful latency experiments (AB tests, p99 tracking), practical use of fallbacks. Communicated tradeoffs well when asked to choose between batching approaches.
- Weaknesses: limited experience with model KV cache semantics (never implemented a KV cache for autoregressive LLMs), tends to conflate single-node microbenchmarks with cluster-wide behavior. Testing story is light: e.g., minimal chaos/latency-injection in prior project.
- Pairing: implemented an example batching dispatcher (pseudocode) and iterated on lock-free queue vs sharded mutex; chosen sharded mutex first, but couldn't fully articulate backpressure handling in extreme load.

Detailed notes (raw, rough):
- Introduced themselves: clear, concise. Good at mapping from problem to metrics.
- On batching: proposes dynamic batch sizing based on latency SLO + queue depth. Suggested per-GPU token budget enforcement which maps nicely to our workload.
- On KV sharing: expects eventual consistency is OK for some caches, but didn't sketch eviction strategy tied to model context size; relied on application-layer TTLs.
- On concurrency: prefers work-stealing thread pools; during pairing, defaulted to worker-per-core with cooperative yielding. Was hesitant to adopt async/await event loop for throughput since they think it complicates backpressure.
- On observability: strong - wants per-path p50/p95/p99 token-time metrics and distribution of sequence lengths; suggested lightweight sampling of KV miss reasons.
- On failures: likes gradual degradation: reduce batch size -> fall back to smaller model variant -> ramp resources. Suggested circuit-breaker by route.
- Culture fit: collaborative, pragmatic, asked good follow-ups. Not super evangelical about building libraries but cares about shipping product-quality systems.

Pairing task specifics:
- Prompt: implement a bounded in-memory prefix cache with concurrent access, support for prefix sharing, and a simple eviction policy.
- Implementation: wrote a sharded hashmap + LRU per shard; used size-based approximate counters. Pseudocode completed for put/get/evict.
- Observed gaps: missing explicit handling of concurrent evict + get race (could return a stale pointer). Candidate suggested atomic reference counting but did not flesh out memory reclamation nor epoch-based reclamation.
- Performance reasoning: used amortized O(1) for get/put; expected throughput fine, but didn't sketch memory footprint accounting for variable-length prefixes.

Scorecard (quick numbers, 1-5):
- System design: 4
- Coding: 3
- Production thinking (SRE/obs/fallbacks): 4
- Collaboration/communication: 5
- Domain familiarity (LLM specifics): 2
- Overall: 3.6

Open questions / follow-ups to ask on a second loop:
- Ask for a specific design that safely handles concurrent evict+reads at scale (expecting epoch/RCU or hazard pointers). See how deep they go into memory reclamation.
- Probe KS/quantization tradeoffs: have them reason about model memory/perf vs quantization artifacts; Dexter's resume didn't show quantization exposure.
- Ask about multi-tenant routing: how they'd map requests to GPU pools to avoid noisy neighbors while meeting latency SLOs.
- Ask for a concrete test plan: unit tests, perf tests, chaos tests for a KV-backed cache.

Risks & mitigation suggestions:
- Risk: weak LLM-KV experience -> could misapply caching invariants and cause consistency bugs in production. Mitigation: pair them with an applied-ML engineer in the next loop and give a short homework: extend the pairing PR to add eviction concurrency tests + perf microbench.
- Risk: might overfit to single-node microbenchmarks and underestimate network effects. Mitigation: during onsite/next loop, include scenario of cross-node cache warmup + churn and ask for routing/backpressure design.

Suggested next-step interviewers and focus areas:
- Applied ML / inference engineer (Maya Singh) — validate model-cache semantics and quality implications.
- SRE / infra (Ibrahim Khan) — validate memory reclamation, chaos resilience, and deployment story.
- Senior runtime architect — deep systems question on epoch-based reclamation vs reference counting; expect a clear decision and tradeoffs.

Recommended homework (short):
- Extend the pairing code to add a simple concurrency test that simulates concurrent put/get/evict and show chosen reclamation strategy. Keep it to ~4-6 hours. Provide a small perf benchmark showing memory growth vs throughput.

Immediate action items (for hiring coordinator):
- If we want to continue: schedule applied-ML loop + SRE loop next week.
- Ask candidate to complete the small homework within 5 business days.
- Tag the loop notes to candidate profile in Greenhouse + attach this doc and pairing PR link.

Notes to self (unpolished):
- I liked how Dexter maps metrics to design choices; good for product-oriented infra.
- Not convinced on memory reclamation — weak signal but fixable with pair-programming.
- Make sure to pressure test with multi-tenant scenarios next round.

Slack shorthand to send to hiring channel: "Dexter Lin: +communication +prod-thinking; needs LLM-cache exposure and concurrency follow-up. Recommend applied-ML + SRE loops + small homework."

End of note.
